title: Greek Sculpture
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek sculptors moved from stiff figures to lifelike bodies.
summary: Archaic kouroi stood stiff and frontal, in a pose reflecting Egypt. Just after 480 BCE the Kritios Boy shifted his weight onto one leg: contrapposto. Polyclitus then wrote the rules.

cards.headline: For generations, Greek statues stood at attention. Then one relaxed.
cards.body: Try it: stand with your weight on one leg, like you're waiting for a bus. Your hips tilt, your shoulders tilt the other way, and you look alive. Greek sculptors had to discover that.

cards.headline: Archaic: the kouros
cards.body: From about 615–590 BCE, Greek sculptors carved kouroi: stone statues of standing young men, some used as grave markers. Picture one facing straight ahead, left foot slightly forward, arms close to his sides, fists clenched. If he reminds you of Egypt, that's no accident: the kouros reflects Egyptian traditions, especially their body proportions. Remember Level 12's grid?

cards.headline: The Kritios Boy shifts his weight
cards.body: Just after 480 BCE, a marble youth from the Athenian Acropolis did something new. He rests his weight on his left leg, while his right leg relaxes, bent at the knee. That's contrapposto: one leg takes the load, so the hips, shoulders and head tilt. Weight on both legs looks like a statue. Weight on one looks like a person.

mascot.line: If you keep one word from this level, make it contrapposto: weight on one leg.

cards.fact: The Spear Bearer was a rulebook you could walk around.
cards.context: About 450–440 BCE, the sculptor Polyclitus made the Doryphoros, or Spear Bearer, to illustrate his book, the Canon, on the ideal proportions of the human body. His relaxed contrapposto helped free Greek sculpture from rigid, face-front poses. The stiff kouros had become a body at ease, measured to an ideal.

cards.headline: Greek sculpture: at ease
learned: Kouroi: stiff, frontal, left foot forward
Kritios Boy: weight on one leg

questions.prompt: Which pose marks an Archaic kouros?

options.label: Weight on one leg, the other knee bent
Twisting to throw, arms raised high
options.rationale: Kouroi keep their arms close to the body.

options.label: Seated on a throne, holding a spear
Facing front, left foot forward, fists clenched

questions.explanation: Early kouroi stand stiffly frontal, left foot slightly forward, arms at their sides and fists clenched.

questions.prompt: Why does contrapposto make a statue look more alive?

options.label: Weight on one leg makes the hips and shoulders tilt
Both feet carry exactly equal weight
options.rationale: That's the stiff pose contrapposto replaced.

options.label: The figure faces straight ahead
options.rationale: Frontality was the old, stiff way.

options.label: The arms are pinned to the sides

questions.explanation: With the weight on one leg, the hips, shoulders and head tilt, the way a real person stands at rest.

questions.prompt: The kouros reflects Egyptian traditions. Which Level 12 idea was it especially indebted to?

options.label: Drawing heads in profile with frontal eyes
options.rationale: That's a rule for flat pictures, not statues.

questions.explanation: Egyptian artists used an 18-unit grid for the body; the kouros reflects Egyptian proportion systems.
